prove.theorem:
Fix k >= 0 and the alphabet [0,k] = {0,...,k}. Words are 0-indexed. A position i is interior if 1 <= i <= L-2. Define:
- A_N: words of length N with no interior strict peak (x_i > x_{i-1} and x_i > x_{i+1});
- V_N: words of length N with no interior strict valley;
- C_N = A_N ∩ V_N;
- B_M: words of length M in which every nonzero letter is <= some existing neighbour;
- D_M: images eps3([0,k]^M) of the clipped 3-window min filter, eps3(w)_i = min{w_j : j in {i-1,i,i+1} ∩ [0,M-1]}.

Theorem 1. For all N >= 1: Phi(x) = delta+(k - x) is a bijection A_N -> B_{N+1}. Here delta+ is the 2-window max filter in full mode with 0-padding, (delta+ x)_i = max of x_{i-1}, x_i over existing indices, i = 0..N. The inverse is y -> k - eps-(y), where eps-(y)_j = min(y_j, y_{j+1}). So |A_N| = |B_{N+1}|, and this also holds for N = 0.
- OEIS: A200886(n,k) = column 1 of Hardin's "n X m 0..k arrays with every nonzero element <= some horizontal or vertical neighbor" table at n+3, for all n, k >= 1.
- In particular, for n >= 1: A200880(n)=A202882(n+3), A200881(n)=A203094(n+3), A200882(n)=A203184(n+3), A200883(n)=A203050(n+3), A200884(n)=A203059(n+3), A200885(n)=A202909(n+3).

Corollary 1. For n >= 1, the number of distinct images of the valid 2-window min filter [0,k]^{n+1} -> [0,k]^n equals |V_n| = |A_n|. Hence A217883(n,2) = A202882(n+1) and A217954(n,2) = A203094(n+1).

Theorem 2. For all N >= 1: eps+ (the 2-window min filter in full mode, top-padded by k) is a bijection C_N -> D_{N+1}, with inverse the valid 2-window max filter delta-. So |C_N| = |D_{N+1}|. This fails for N = 0.
- OEIS: A200871(n,k) = D(n+3,k) for all n, k >= 1. In particular A200865(n) = A217450(n+3) and A200866(n) = A218051(n+3) for n >= 1.
- The same holds for column 1 of A217457, A217645 and A217547 (and column 2 of A217547), and for column 1 of A218181, A218651 and A218056 (and column 2 of A218056).

Theorem 3. For every k >= 0, sum_{N>=0} |A_N| x^N = b_k(x^2)/(b_k(x^2) - x B_k(x^2)) and sum_{n>=1} |B_n| x^n = x b_k(x^2)/(b_k(x^2) - x B_k(x^2)). Here b_k(y) = sum_j C(k+j,2j) y^j and B_k(y) = sum_j C(k+1+j,2j+1) y^j. Hence for N >= 2k+1, A(N) = sum_{j=1}^{2k+1} (-1)^{j+1} C(k+1+floor((j-1)/2), j) A(N-j).

Also proved (rigorous finite certificates): all 102 Empirical or conjectured formulas stored in A200865-A200877, A200880-A200892, A202882, A203094, A203184, A203050, A203059, A202909, A217450 and A218051.
prove.proof_summary:
Theorem 1: three lattice facts on 2-window filters.
- The valid erosion eps- has image V_N, and eps- delta+ fixes exactly V_N, via min(max(a,b),max(b,c)) = max(b,min(a,c)).
- The full 0-padded dilation delta+ has image exactly B_{N+1}, and delta+ eps- fixes B_{N+1}.
- Complementation x -> k-x swaps A_N and V_N.
So Phi = delta+ ∘ complement and Psi = complement ∘ eps- are inverse bijections A_N <-> B_{N+1}.

Theorem 2:
- The clipped 3-window erosion factors as eps3 = eps+ ∘ eps-, so D_{N+1} = eps+(V_N).
- delta- eps+ only lowers strict peaks to the higher neighbour, so it fixes A_N and maps V_N into V_N ∩ A_N = C_N. A case check shows lowering a strict peak never creates a strict valley.
- eps+ delta- eps+ = eps+.
Hence eps+ restricted to C_N is a bijection onto D_{N+1}, with inverse delta-.

Theorem 3: factor a B-word at its zeros. With E = g.f. of words in which every letter has a >= neighbour, this gives F_k = E_{k-1}/(1 - x E_{k-1}) and E_k = F_k - x. That is a Möbius recursion, which matches Mansour-Shattuck Lemma 2.1 at q = 0. It is solved by Morgan-Voyce polynomials using only Pascal's rule.

The remaining stored formulas for the peak-and-valley family (k <= 7) and the row polynomials are proved by Cayley-Hamilton on explicit transfer matrices (dimension 3(k+1)) and by polynomiality in k (standardisation of words).

novelty.prior_art:
1) Mansour & Shattuck, "Counting Peaks and Valleys in a Partition of a Set", J. Integer Seq. 13 (2010), Art. 10.6.8, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Shattuck/shattuck3.html (TeX: .../shattuck3.tex).
- Peaks are interior strict peaks: "a peak ... is an entry pi_j, 1<=j<=n-2, of pi such that pi_j<pi_{j+1}>pi_{j+2}".
- Corollary 2.5 (numbered with the theorem counter): "The generating function W_k(x,0) for the number of words of length n over the alphabet [k] without peaks is given by W_k(x,0)=(U_{k-1}(t)-U_{k-2}(t))/((1-x)U_{k-1}(t)-U_{k-2}(t)), where t=1+x^2/2".
- I checked symbolically for k=0..6 that B_k(y)=U_k(1+y/2) and b_k(y)=U_k(1+y/2)-U_{k-1}(1+y/2). So the A-part of Theorem 3 is exactly M-S Corollary 2.5 with k -> k+1. Lemma 2.1 is their Möbius recursion, and Remark 2.4 is the peaks/valleys complement.

2) OEIS A202882 (B-words over 0..2). R. J. Mathar added a link on Jul 09 2017 (history #6): "T. Mansour and M. Shattuck, Counting Peaks and Valleys in a Partition of a Set, J. Int. Seq. 13 (2010), 10.6.8, Lemma 2.1, k=3, one peak." The words "one peak" look like a slip: A202882(n) equals the number of peak-free words of length n-1 over [3] (1,3,9,22,51,...), which I checked by brute force.

3) OEIS A203094 (B-words over 0..3). Same Mathar link, Jul 09 2017 (history #10): "... Lemma 2.1, k=4, no peak." Its own %F is "Empirical: G.f.: -x*(1+6*x^2+5*x^4+x^6)/(...)". This is x times W_4(x,0).
- Taken together, items 2 and 3 already assert in OEIS, with no proof, that B-counts are shifted peak-free word counts for k=2,3.
- That makes A200880(n)=A202882(n+3) and A200881(n)=A203094(n+3) immediate, because A200880 and A200881 are peak-free counts by definition. Neither entry cross-references A200880 or A200881.
- Nothing comparable exists for k=4..7 (A203184, A203050, A203059, A202909).

4) OEIS A005251 (the k=1 case of Theorem 1):
- "a(n+3) is the number of n-bit sequences that avoid 010. - David Callan, Mar 25 2004"
- "For n >= 2, a(n) is the number of (n-2)-length binary words with no isolated zeros. - Milan Janjic, Mar 07 2015"
- "For n>=3, a(n) is the number of binary strings of length n-2 without any maximal runs of ones of length 1. - Félix Balado, Aug 25 2025"
- Link "... Lemma 2.1, k=2, 0 peaks."
- A200886 says "Column 1 is A005251(n+5)".
- So |A_N| = A005251(N+3) = |B_{N+1}| for k=1.

5) Corollary 1's OEIS consequences are already stated, as observations by R. H. Hardin (2012), not proved:
- A217883: "Column 2 is A202882(n+1)."
- A217954: "Column 2 is A203094(n+1)."

6) The k=1 case of Theorem 2 is implicit, because both families cite A006355:
- A200871: "Column 1 is A006355(n+4)"
- A217637 (0..1 min-of-neighbours table): "Columns 1-3 are A006355(n+1), A217631, A217632."
- I found nothing for k>=2: no link between A200865 and A217450, or between A200866 and A218051, or any other column.

7) A200886 rows: "T(n,k) is the number of lattice points in k*P ... an Ehrhart polynomial of degree n+2. This confirms the empirical formulas for the rows. - Robert Israel, Mar 21 2021". So the row formulas of A200886 were already proved.

8) Background, not this identity:
- That a dilation restricted to the image of its adjoint erosion is a bijection onto the dilation's image (with the erosion as inverse) is the standard Galois-connection/adjunction fact of lattice theory and mathematical morphology.
- C_N is exactly the root set of the window-3 median filter (Gallagher-Wise 1981, Arce-Gallagher 1982; Maragos-Schafer relate median roots to open-closed signals).
- I found no source that counts these roots against images of the 3-window erosion.

What is already known:
- **Theorem 3** is known: it is Mansour-Shattuck 2010 Corollary 2.5 with k -> k+1, in Chebyshev form, since Morgan-Voyce B_k(y)=U_k(1+y/2) and b_k=U_k-U_{k-1}. The order-(2k+1) recurrences of A200880-A200885 follow directly. The B-series g.f. is then just x times that.
- **Theorem 1, k=1:** known through A005251, whose comments give both the "avoid 010" and the "no isolated zeros / no runs of ones of length 1" readings.
- **Theorem 1, k=2,3:** effectively stated in OEIS since 2017, with no proof. R. J. Mathar's links on A202882 ("Lemma 2.1, k=3, one peak", apparently meaning no peak) and A203094 ("Lemma 2.1, k=4, no peak") identify the B-sequences as shifted peak-free-word counts. Given the A-sequences' definitions, A200880(n)=A202882(n+3) and A200881(n)=A203094(n+3) follow immediately. The B-side g.f.s are still marked "Empirical", and nothing cross-references A200880/A200881.
- **Corollary 1:** its OEIS statements are already in A217883 and A217954 as Hardin's "Column 2 is A202882(n+1)" and "Column 2 is A203094(n+1)", unproved.
- **Theorem 2, k=1:** implicit through A006355, which A200871 and A217637 both cite.
- **Row formulas of A200886:** already proved by Robert Israel's Ehrhart-polynomial comment.
- **The lattice mechanism:** that a dilation restricted to the image of its adjoint erosion is a bijection onto its own image is a textbook adjunction fact.

What I could not find anywhere:
1. The explicit bijection Phi(x)=delta+(k-x) from A_N to B_{N+1}, and the general-k identity |A_N|=|B_{N+1}|. In particular, nothing links A200882-A200885 to A203184, A203050, A203059, A202909, and nothing links the A200886 table to Hardin's "every nonzero element <= some neighbor" tables.
2. Theorem 2 for k>=2: the bijection from peak-and-valley-free words C_N (the roots of the window-3 median filter) onto images of the clipped 3-window min filter D_{N+1}. Hence A200871(n,k)=D(n+3,k), A200865(n)=A217450(n+3) and A200866(n)=A218051(n+3). The same goes for the related columns of A217457, A217645, A217547, A218181, A218651 and A218056. Corollaries:
- A228016(n) = 11a(n-1) - 11a(n-2) + a(n-3) for all n>=4.
- sum_{n>=1} a(n) x^{n-1} = (54-55x+5x^2)/(1-11x+11x^2-x^3). This is Kimberling's g.f., which uses the offset-0 convention. Equivalently, sum_{n>=1} a(n) x^n = x(54-55x+5x^2)/((1-x)(1-10x+x^2)).

prove.proof_summary:
(a) A Pell-equation argument. 3k(k+1)+1 = m(m+1)/2 is equivalent to (2m+1)^2 - 6(2k+1)^2 = 3. By descent with the unit 5+2sqrt6, every positive solution has the form (3+sqrt6)(5+2sqrt6)^j. This gives Y_{j+2} = 10Y_{j+1} - Y_j, so k_j = (Y_j - 1)/2 = e_j.

(b) Put b_n = e_n + 1/2. Then b_n = 10b_{n-1} - b_{n-2}, the invariant b_{n-1}^2 - b_n b_{n-2} = 3 holds, and the ratios satisfy rho_n = b_n/b_{n-1} in (9, 11], with rho_n < 10 for n>=2.

Let D(m) = H(m) - log(m+1/2) - C = sum_{k>m} g(k), where g(k) = log((k+1/2)/(k-1/2)) - 1/k = 2 sum_{j>=1} t^{2j+1}/(2j+1) with t = 1/(2k). Compare g(k) termwise with the telescoping differences of 1/(24x^2) and of 1/(24x^2) - 1/(120x^4). The lower comparison reduces to the polynomial inequality 2s + 42s^2 - 4s^3 - 14s^4 + 6s^5 >= 0 for s in (0, 1/4]. This gives, for every m>=0 with beta = m+1/2:
1/(24beta^2) - 1/(120beta^4) < D(m) < 1/(24beta^2).

Then H(e_n) - T_n = log(1 - 3/v^2) + D(e_n) + D(e_{n-2}) - 2D(e_{n-1}). For n>=3, with u = b_{n-2} >= 11/2 and v = rho·u, rho > 9, this gives 24u^2(H(e_n) - T_n) > 1 - (4/605 + 2/81 + 8712/9789) > 0.0787. Also T_n - H(e_n - 1) > 1/e_n - 1/(24u^2) > 0, because e_n < 110u <= 24u^2.

The only case checked by direct computation is n=2: H(53) < 137/30 < H(54). It is verified in exact rationals and also by hand.

(c) Induction from (b), using the strict monotonicity of H.

Section 3. The series for g(k), with t = 1/(2k), is right. Telescoping identity (3.2) is right. In Lemma 3.1 I re-derived both closed forms. The upper bound follows from comparing coefficients ((j+1)/3 against 1/(2j+3), equal only at j = 0). For the lower bound, P(s) is expanded correctly and is positive on (0, 1/4]. Lemma 3.2 then follows by summing and telescoping, and the strict inequalities survive the limit because the termwise differences are positive.

Section 4. The n = 2 case is checked exactly: H(53) < 137/30 < H(54), and the fractions match. For n >= 3: u >= 11/2, rho in (9, 11], rho_n < 10, and uw = v^2 - 3 are all valid. In the right inequality, -log(1-x) <= x/(1-x) and the (3.4) bounds go in the correct directions, the scaled expression is correct, and the constant bound 12587353/159903315 > 0.0787 is correct. Section 5. The induction from c_{-1} = e_0 and c_0 = e_1 is correct. Because both inequalities are strict, the '<=' reading gives the same terms. So does Ceiling of the exact real root, since H is increasing on (-1, infinity).

prove.theorem: Let A112046(i) = f(2i+1), where f(m) = least k >= 1 with Jacobi(k,m) != +1 (m odd >= 3). Let A112051 be defined by a(1)=1 and a(n) = first index i > a(n-1) with A112046(i) not in {A112046(1..a(n-1))} (offset 1). Let A216244(n) = (prime(n)^2-1)/2 (offset 2). Theorem 1: A112051(1..3) = 1, 3, 11, and A112051(n) = (prime(n)^2-1)/2 = A216244(n) for every n >= 4. The identity fails at n = 2, 3, where A216244 gives 4 and 12. Equivalently, A112052(n) = prime(n)^2 for n >= 4, and A112051(n) = A084921(n) for n >= 4. The key ingredient is Theorem 2: for every odd prime q, the least quadratic non-residue n(q) satisfies n(q)^2 < q, except for q = 3, 7, 23. As a corollary, f(m)^2 > m for odd m >= 3 holds only when m is 3, 7 or 23.
prove.proof_summary:
Reduction: f(m) is always prime, and f(p^2) = p. If f(m) = p and m < p^2, then every k < p is coprime to m. If p | m, then m = p, which is impossible because there are non-residues below p. Otherwise every prime factor of m is > p, so m is a prime q with n(q) = p > sqrt(q). So the first occurrence of each prime p >= 7 in A112046 is at index (p^2-1)/2, provided Theorem 2 holds. A112051 lists the first-occurrence positions in increasing order, which gives Theorem 1.

Theorem 2 has a fully elementary proof. The classical argument gives n(n-1) < q. If also q < n^2, then r = q - n(n-1) lies in [1, n-1], which forces chi(-1) = -1. So every integer in [q-n+1, q-1] is a non-residue. For n >= 29, take N = (q-n+2)/2, s = ceil(sqrt N) and t = floor(sqrt(s^2-N)), and set a = s-t, b = s+t. Then ab = s^2 - t^2 lies in [N, N+2t], with t < 2^(1/4) sqrt(n). Explicit inequalities, checked exactly at n = 29 and shown monotone above it, give 1 <= a <= b <= n-1 and q-n+2 <= 2ab <= q-1. So 2ab is a residue (a product of numbers below n) lying in the all-non-residue window: a contradiction. The remaining primes n <= 23 (so q < 529) are checked by hand. Since q must be 7 mod 8, the only candidates are q = 47, 167 and 359, and none of them works. That leaves exactly the exceptions 3, 7, 23. Separately, Trevino's bound n(q) <= 1.1 q^(1/4) log q, combined with the computations, gives a second proof of Theorem 2.

I tried to refute the claim and could not. Every definition, offset, lemma and constant checks out.

Definitions and offsets (taken from the OEIS snapshot entries):
- A112046 has offset 1: a(n) = least k with J(k,2n+1) != +1, so A112046(i)=f(2i+1).
- A112051 has offset 1: a(1)=1, then the first new-value index after a(n-1).
- A216244 has offset 2: (prime(n)^2-1)/2. A112051(n)=A216244(n) uses the same n, e.g. A112051(4)=24=A216244(4) with prime(4)=7.
- A112052 = 2*A112051+1 (offset 1). A084921(n) = (prime(n)^2-1)/2 for n>=2.

Section 1 (reduction to Theorem 2):
- Lemma 1.1 (values are prime): correct by multiplicativity.
- Lemma 1.2 (f(p^2)=p): correct, since J(k,p^2)=J(k,p)^2.
- Proposition 1.3:
  - From J(k,m)=1 for k<p, every prime factor of m is >= p.
  - Case J(p,m)=0 forces m=p. That contradicts the existence of non-residues mod an odd prime.
  - Case J(p,m)=-1 makes m prime: two prime factors would both be >p, giving m>p^2. Then p=n(q).
- Corollary 1.4: first(2,3,5)=1,3,11 matches the data. For p>=7, any i<(p^2-1)/2 with f(2i+1)=p would force 2i+1 to be 3, 7 or 23, whose f-values are 2, 3, 5. Monotonicity holds.
- Lemma 1.5: A112051 enumerates first-occurrence positions. The induction is correct.
- Theorem 1 follows.

Section 2 (Theorem 2):
- Lemma A: m=ceil(q/n) satisfies m<q and chi(m)=-1, so m>=n. Correct.
- Lemma B: r=q-n(n-1) lies in [1,n-1] and r is congruent to -n(n-1), so chi(-1)=-1, and [q-n+1,q-1] consists of non-residues. Correct.
- Lemma C (purely arithmetic):
  - N=(q-n+2)/2 is an integer because n and q are odd.
  - D<=2s-2, t^2<=D<=t^2+2t, and N<=ab<=N+2t all hold.
  - a>=1 because t<s.
  - Size bounds: s<n/sqrt2+1, D<sqrt2*n, t<2^(1/4)sqrt(n).
  - b<=n-1 reduces to g(n)>=0, and g increases for n>=5 with g(29)>0.
  - 4t<=n-3 reduces to phi(n)>=0, and phi increases past 14.3 with phi(29)>0.
- Main step: chi(2ab)=1 because 2, a and b are all below n. Since q-n+2<=2ab<=q-1, Lemma B gives chi(2ab)=-1, a contradiction for n>=29.
- Hand check for n<=23:
  - n=2,3,5 give exactly q=3,7,23.
  - For n in {7,11,13,17,19,23}, Lemma B forces q to be 7 mod 8. The prime lists for each interval are correct, and only 47, 167, 359 qualify. Their small non-residues (5, 5, 7) are confirmed: (5/47)=(5/167)=(7/359)=-1.
  - Primes 23<n<29 do not exist, so the finite check covers exactly the cases the argument leaves open.

Side claims:
- A112052 is a square of a prime from n=4 on.
- A112049's first occurrences are records.
- For A112060, f(p^2 r^2)=p for primes r>p, and f(m)=2 for m congruent to 3 or 5 mod 8, so every prime occurs infinitely often.
These are all correct.

The colleague's stated computations (60 terms below 40000, A112051(9592)=4999100040, the 2,000,909 Lemma C pairs, the failing n list) were all reproduced independently. My own computations go further: A112051 literally up to index 1e10 (13132 terms), and the f(m)^2>m claim for all odd m up to 1e14.

1) Theorem 2 is classical. The abstract of H. J. Godwin, "On the least quadratic non-residue", Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 61 (1965) 671-672, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100039025, reads verbatim: "If n(p) is the least quadratic non-residue of a given prime p then it is known ((1)) that n(p) = O(p^α) for any α > 1/(4 √e). LeVeque ((2), page 122) gives the following bound with an explicit constant: n(p) < √p for p ≠ 2, 3, 7, 23. In the present paper an elementary and self-contained proof is given of a result slightly stronger than LeVeque's. Some numerical results, which indicate the extent to which the result proved falls short of what actually obtains, are appended." Here (2) is W. J. LeVeque, Topics in Number Theory, vol. 1 (1956), p. 122. This is exactly Theorem 2 ("n(q)^2 < q except q = 3, 7, 23"), already with an elementary proof. Godwin's paper is linked from OEIS A000229, the sequence of least primes q with n(q) = prime(n): "a(n) is the least number m such that the n-th prime is the least quadratic nonresidue modulo m." Theorem 2 is equivalent to A000229(n) > prime(n)^2 for n >= 4, though A000229 never states this. Also relevant: A053760 cites Trevino's bound n(p) < 1.1 p^(1/4) log p for p > 3 and the weaker bound a(n) < 1 + sqrt(p). Hummel (arXiv math/0305298) quotes Brauer: for p ≡ 3 (mod 4), runs of residues or non-residues are shorter than sqrt(p).
2) The identity itself is still marked as a conjecture in OEIS. A112052 (2*A112051+1) says: "From n>=4 onward seems to be squares of primes (A001248)." A112049 has a comment by Karttunen, May 26 2017: "A112051 gives the first positions of distinct new values in this sequence, that seem also to be the positions of the first occurrence of each n, and thus the positions of the records. Compare also to A084921." No proof, draft or pending edit exists, and I found no paper or website that states A112051(n) = (prime(n)^2-1)/2 or A112052(n) = prime(n)^2 for n >= 4. A281680 has a similar-looking comment ("First occurrence of the k-th prime ... is at n = 4, 12, 24, 60, ... This appears to be either A084921 or A216244"), but it is about smallest prime factors and is unrelated.
novelty.details:
The hard part of the result, Theorem 2 (n(q) < sqrt(q) for every odd prime q except 3, 7, 23), is classical. LeVeque stated it in Topics in Number Theory vol. 1 (1956), p. 122, and Godwin (1965) gave an elementary, self-contained proof of a slightly stronger result. Godwin's paper is even linked from OEIS A000229. The second proof suggested in the task (Trevino's bound plus a computation) is also only a combination of known results.

What is new is the application to Karttunen's sequences. Theorem 1 says A112051(n) = A216244(n) = (prime(n)^2-1)/2 for n >= 4; equivalently A112052(n) = prime(n)^2 and A112051(n) = A084921(n) for n >= 4. OEIS still lists this as a conjecture ("seems to be squares of primes" in A112052; "seem also to be ... Compare also to A084921" in A112049), and I found no source that proves or even states it as a theorem.

The step from the known result to Theorem 1 is short and elementary:
- f(m) is always prime (already noted in A112046), and f(p^2) = p.
- If f(m) = p and m < p^2, then m must be a prime q with n(q) = p > sqrt(q).
- So the first odd modulus with f = p is min(p^2, A000229(pi(p))). By Godwin/LeVeque this equals p^2 for every p >= 7.
- A112051 records these first occurrences in increasing order, which gives Theorem 1.

So the OEIS identity is not written down anywhere, but it follows in a few lines from a known 1956/1965 theorem. That is why I classify it as PARTIALLY_KNOWN rather than NEW. A good OEIS write-up would turn the A112052/A112049 conjectures into a theorem citing Godwin 1965 and LeVeque, and could add to A000229 the remark "a(n) > prime(n)^2 for n >= 4 (Godwin/LeVeque)". I checked the claims numerically in PARI (first occurrences for i <= 200000; Theorem 2 for primes up to 10^7). Downloaded PDFs and text extracts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-test1/92b0ad82-0425-5b2b-85ed-b7d12d7491b1/scratchpad/pdf/, and the Godwin abstract HTML is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-test1/92b0ad82-0425-5b2b-85ed-b7d12d7491b1/scratchpad/godwin.html.

prove.theorem:
Definitions. A282297 and A282295 are rule 451. A279721 and A279720 are rule 193. Both are Wolfram-coded outer-totalistic CAs on the 5-cell von Neumann neighbourhood: new state = bit_{c+2s}(code), where c is the centre state and s is the number of ON neighbours. Each starts from a single ON cell at stage 0. Offset 0: a(n) is the 0/1 string of x-axis cells at stage n, read as a decimal number. A282297 and A279721 read x = 0..n; A282295 and A279720 read x = -n..0.

Result: both conjectures (a(n) = A279721(n) and a(n) = A279720(n) for n >= 2) are FALSE.
- A282297(26) = 111100000000000111111111111, but A279721(26) = 111000000000000111111111111.
- A282295(26) = 111111111111000000000001111, but A279720(26) = 111111111111000000000000111.
- For 2 <= n <= 25 both pairs agree. For n = 1 and every 26 <= n <= 1000 both pairs differ. So n = 26 is the first counterexample.
- The two conjectures are equivalent to each other for each n, by D4 symmetry: the left readout is the reversal of the right one.
prove.proof_summary:
From the Mathematica program, T_193(c,s)=1 iff (c=0 and s=0) or s=3, and T_451(c,s)=1 iff s=0 or s=3 or (c=0 and s=4). The rules differ only on two inputs: an isolated ON cell (1,0) and a fully surrounded OFF cell (0,4).

By hand, the two configurations coincide at stage 2. They stay identical through stage 16. Then isolated ON cells at (+-2,+-2) make them differ at stage 17. The differences heal twice (stages 18 and 23) and from stage 24 on persist.

A hand-checkable local certificate settles n = 26. It starts from the common stage-23 configuration on the 25-cell diamond |x-3|+|y| <= 3. At stage 24, cells (3,+-1) are isolated ON cells in both evolutions; rule 451 keeps them ON and rule 193 turns them OFF. So at stage 26 the axis cell (3,0) sees s=3 under rule 451 (index 7, ON) and s=1 under rule 193 (index 3, OFF).

Supporting lemmas:
- The 257-torus equals the plane for n <= 126 (light-cone bound 257-126 = 131 > 126).
- D4 symmetry carries the result to x = -3 and makes the two conjectures equivalent.

Minimality (agreement for 2 <= n <= 25) is a finite check, confirmed by the OEIS b-files and three independent simulators.

I tried to refute the claim and could not. Both conjectures are false, and n = 26 is the first counterexample.

**Definitions.**
- The %O lines are 0,2 for A282297 and 0,3 for the other three, so the offset is 0, as claimed.
- 193 = 2^7+2^6+2^0 and 451 = 2^8+2^7+2^6+2^1+2^0.
- The rule[[10-v]] lookup gives bit v of the code, with v = c + 2s.
- The decoded Boolean forms are correct. The two rules differ only on the inputs (1,0) and (0,4), where rule 451 gives 1 and rule 193 gives 0.
- In Price's Mathematica program, the right readout uses Range[i,2i-1] (x = 0..n) and the left readout uses Range[1,i] (x = -n..0), at stage i-1.
- The live OEIS entries still carry Mathar's %F conjectures, dated Jun 21 2025.

**Lemma 1 (background).** The background is b_t = t mod 2, because T(0,0) = bit 0 = 1 and T(1,4) = bit 9 = 0 for both codes. The diamond induction is correct. My exact computation confirms it through stage 60.

**Lemma 2 (torus equals plane on the readout cells).** The lifting argument is correct, and the bound 257 - 126 = 131 > n holds. My exact plane computation, which uses no torus, agrees with the 257-torus replica for all n <= 126.

**Lemma 3 (D4 symmetry).** The rule depends on the neighbours only through their count, and the seed is D4-invariant. Each readout has fixed length n+1, so dropping leading zeros cannot make two different strings equal. The equivalence of the two conjectures follows. I checked D4 invariance on the full configurations and on all four axis readouts up to n = 1000.

**Lemma 4 (stages 1 and 2).** I checked every case by hand:
- At stage 1 only the origin differs.
- At stage 2, the origin is (0,0)→1 under rule 193 and (1,0)→1 under rule 451. Cell (1,0) is (0,3)→1 and (0,4)→1. Cell (2,0) is (1,3)→1 and cell (1,1) is (1,2)→0.
- Every remaining cell has c = 1 and s >= 2.

The stage-16 isolated ON cells are at (±2,±2) and they cause the 4 differing cells at stage 17. Isolated ON cells also appear at stages 20 and 23, which explains the counts 12 at stage 21 and 16 at stage 24. The table of difference counts is exact.

**Section 5 certificate.** I checked every row of the stage-24, stage-25 and stage-26 tables by hand from the stated stage-23 diamond, and also by simulation. Cell (3,1) at stage 24 is an isolated ON cell, so it becomes 1 under rule 451 and 0 under rule 193 at stage 25. That makes (3,0) at stage 26 have index 7 (gives 1) under rule 451 and index 3 (gives 0) under rule 193. This is the only differing digit, x = 3, of R(26).

**Counts.** 102 = 1 + 101 and 976 = 1 + 975 are both correct.

**Finite check.** The b-files settle n <= 126, and they are the authoritative source: the counterexample n = 26 and its minimality are there directly. The extension to 1000 is extra, and I confirmed it with a method that assumes nothing about the background or the torus.

Only the minor presentational notes listed under gaps remain.

Nobody has explicitly stated that Mathar's conjectures are false.
- The live entries still carry the conjectures: "Conjecture: a(n) = A279721(n) for n>=2. - _R. J. Mathar_, Jun 21 2025" (https://oeis.org/A282297) and "Conjecture: a(n) = A279720(n) for n>=2. - _R. J. Mathar_, Jun 21 2025" (https://oeis.org/A282295).
- Edit histories end with Sean A. Irvine's link-only global edit of Nov 05 2025. No refuting edit, comment or draft exists.
- No paper, arXiv preprint or web page mentions the pair.

But the counterexample has been in published OEIS data since 2016/2017, years before the conjecture:
1. Robert Price's b-files (n=0..126) give A282297(26)=111100000000000111111111111 vs A279721(26)=111000000000000111111111111, and A282295(26)=111111111111000000000001111 vs A279720(26)=111111111111000000000000111. The b-file pairs differ exactly at n=1 and n=26..126.
2. More visibly, the data sections of the decimal companions (the same readouts in base 10) already show the discrepancy at n=26:
   - A282298 (rule 451, left) has "...,33546247,15608,134184975,..." and A279722 (rule 193, left) has "...,33546247,15608,134184967,...".
   - A282299 (rule 451, right) has "...,29364223,8187904,125833215,..." and A279723 (rule 193, right) has "...,29364223,8187904,117444607,...".
   - 134184975 and 134184967 are the decimal values of the two left n=26 strings; 125833215 and 117444607 are those of the right strings.
   - https://oeis.org/A282298, https://oeis.org/A279722, https://oeis.org/A282299, https://oeis.org/A279723
3. The ON-cell counts A272256 (rule 451) and A270685 (rule 193) match for 2 <= n <= 16 and first differ at n=17 (852 vs 848). They match again at 18-20 and 23 and differ at 21-22 and from 24 on. This is exactly the divergence-and-healing pattern in the result.

Analogous but different pair: the rule 449 entries carry Robert Price-style comments against rule 193. A282265 says "Similar to A279720 but differing starting at a(30)". A282266 says "Similar to A272721 but differing beginning at a(30)" (a typo for A279721). A282267 and A282268 say the same against A279722 and A279723. No such comment exists for rule 451.
novelty.details:
The refutation is correct. I checked it against the OEIS b-files and an independent torus simulation, exact for n <= 1000.
- A282297(26) ≠ A279721(26) and A282295(26) ≠ A279720(26).
- Both pairs agree for 2 <= n <= 25 and differ at n=1 and for every n from 26 to 1000.
- The full configurations differ at stage 17, agree at 18-20, differ at 21-22, agree at 23, and differ from 24 on. This matches the "heals at 18 and 23" claim (it does not mention the differences at 21-22).
- The rule analysis is consistent with the Wolfram codes. 193 = bits {0,6,7} and 451 = bits {0,1,6,7,8}, so the two rules differ only on (c,s) = (1,0) and (0,4).

Why not NEW:
- No source states that the conjectures are false, gives the first counterexample, or offers the local certificate. In that sense the explicit refutation, minimality at n=26 and the mechanism are new.
- However, the counterexample sits in OEIS data published in 2016/2017, before Mathar's June 2025 conjecture. It is in the four b-files, and even in the visible data sections of the decimal companions that the binary entries' own Cf. lines list (A282298/A282299). For example, A282298(26)=134184975 vs A279722(26)=134184967.
- So the falsity follows at once from existing OEIS data. Mathar evidently compared only the short binary data sections, which end at n=22/23.

Why not KNOWN: the conjectures are still live, unrefuted and uncommented in the OEIS. The closest explicit statement is the analogous rule 449 vs rule 193 note "differing starting at a(30)" in A282265-A282268, which concerns a different rule.
